question.knowledge_point: Finding a Quadratic Polynomial Given Two Real Roots and a Leading Coefficient
question.problem: The quadratic polynomial $P(t)$ has roots ${t}_{1}=-5,{t}_{2}=5,$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $4.$ Find $P(t).$
question.worked_solution:
Since our quadratic polynomial has roots ${t}_{1}=-5$ and ${t}_{2}=5,$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=4,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t-{t}_{1})(t-{t}_{2}) & =(4)(t-(-5))(t-5) \\  & =4(t+5)(t-5)\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}4(t+5)(t-5) & =4({t}^{2}-25) \\  & =4{t}^{2}-100.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(t)=4{t}^{2}-100.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding a Quadratic Polynomial Given a Double Root and a Leading Coefficient
question.problem: The quadratic polynomial $P(y)$ has the double root ${y}_{1}={y}_{2}=4,$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=3.$ Find $P(y).$
question.worked_solution:
Since our quadratic polynomial has the double root ${y}_{1}={y}_{2}=4,$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=3,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(y-{y}_{1})^{2} & =3{(y-4)}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{(y-4)}^{2} & =3({y}^{2}-8y+16) \\  & =3{y}^{2}-24y+48.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(y)=3{y}^{2}-24y+48.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding a Quadratic Polynomial Given Two Imaginary or Complex Roots
question.problem: The quadratic polynomial $f(x)$ has real coefficients, has roots ${x}_{1}=6\text{i}$ and ${x}_{2}=-6\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $1.$ Find $f(x).$
question.worked_solution:
Since our quadratic polynomial has roots ${x}_{1}=6\text{i}$ and ${x}_{2}=-6\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=1,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2}) & =(1)(x-6\text{i})(x-(-6\text{i})) \\  & =(x-6\text{i})(x+6\text{i})\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-6\text{i})(x+6\text{i}) & ={x}^{2}-(6\text{i})^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-36{\text{i}}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}+36.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)={x}^{2}+36.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding a Quadratic Polynomial Given Two Imaginary or Complex Roots
question.problem: The quadratic polynomial $f(z)$ has real coefficients, has roots ${z}_{1}=3+2\text{i}$ and ${z}_{2}=3-2\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $-2.$ Find $f(z).$
question.worked_solution:
Since our quadratic polynomial has roots ${z}_{1}=3+2\text{i}$ and ${z}_{2}=3-2\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=-2,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(z-{z}_{1})(z-{z}_{2}) & =(-2)(z-(3+2\text{i}))(z-(3-2\text{i}))\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2)(z-(3+2\text{i}))(z-(3-2\text{i})) & =(-2)({z}^{2}-(3+2\text{i})z-(3-2\text{i})z+(3+2\text{i})(3-2\text{i})) \\  & =(-2)({z}^{2}-(3+2\text{i}+3-2\text{i})z+({3}^{2}-{2}^{2}{\text{i}}^{2})) \\  & =(-2)({z}^{2}-6z+(9+4)) \\  & =-2{z}^{2}+12z-26.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=-2{z}^{2}+12z-26.$

question.knowledge_point: Factoring a Quadratic Polynomial With Complex Roots
question.problem: Which of the following is a factor of ${u}^{2}-2u+5?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we let $f(u)={u}^{2}-2u+5.$

Next, we solve $f(u)=0$ by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(u) & =0 \\ {u}^{2}-2u+5 & =0 \\ ({u}^{2}-2\cdot u+{1}^{2})-{1}^{2}+5 & =0 \\ (u-1)^{2}+4 & =0 \\ (u-1)^{2} & =-4 \\ (u-1)^{2} & =4{\text{i}}^{2} \\ (u-1)^{2} & =(2\text{i})^{2} \\ u-1 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ u & =1\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Since our quadratic equation has roots ${u}_{1}=1+2\text{i}$ and ${u}_{2}=1-2\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=1,$ the expression ${u}^{2}-2u+5$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-2u+5 & =a(u-{u}_{1})(u-{u}_{2}) \\  & =(u-(1+2\text{i}))(u-(1-2\text{i})).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, among the given options, only $u-(1-2\text{i})$ is a factor of ${u}^{2}-2u+5.$

question.knowledge_point: Factoring a Quadratic Polynomial With Complex Roots
question.problem: Which of the following is a factor of $3{z}^{2}-24z+75?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we let $f(z)=3{z}^{2}-24z+75.$

Next, we solve $f(z)=0$ by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(z) & =0 \\ 3{z}^{2}-24z+75 & =0 \\ {z}^{2}-8z+25 & =0 \\ ({z}^{2}-2\cdot 4\cdot z+{4}^{2})-{4}^{2}+25 & =0 \\ (z-4)^{2}-16+25 & =0 \\ (z-4)^{2}+9 & =0 \\ (z-4)^{2} & =-9 \\ (z-4)^{2} & =9{\text{i}}^{2} \\ (z-4)^{2} & =(3\text{i})^{2} \\ z-4 & =\pm 3\text{i} \\ z & =4\pm 3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Since our quadratic equation has roots ${z}_{1}=4+3\text{i}$ and ${z}_{2}=4-3\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=3,$ the expression $3{z}^{2}-24z+75$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}3{z}^{2}-24z+75 & =a(z-{z}_{1})(z-{z}_{2}) \\  & =3(z-(4+3\text{i}))(z-(4-3\text{i})).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, among the given options, only $z-(4-3\text{i})$ is a factor of $3{z}^{2}-24z+75.$
